title: Gilpin County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Gilpin County wells have a median depth of 250 ft and reported yield of 7.0 gpm. Compare drilling costs, bedrock conditions and buying risks.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Gilpin County
intro_html:
A well budget in Gilpin County starts with fractured bedrock, not a predictable layer of sand holding water. The countywide median depth is 250 feet, with a modeled finished-well cost of $22,200-$37,000 at that depth. Neither figure guarantees what a particular lot will need.

Colorado DWR records include 4,554 permitted wells across the county. For property around Rollinsville or Black Hawk, nearby completion records and a current pumping test are more useful than a county average alone.

sections.heading: Why a Gilpin County Bid Needs Room Beyond 250 Feet
sections.html:
Among 3,309 wells reporting depth, the median is 250 feet, and the middle half runs 150-380 feet. That spread matters when comparing bids: a contractor pricing only the median depth may leave substantial additional footage outside the base price. Ask how deeper drilling and additional casing would be charged.

Gilpin County is fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer; Denver Basin aquifer wells account for 0%. Water depends on the fractures the borehole intersects. The 90th-percentile depth is 523 feet, showing why a shallower neighboring well is useful evidence, but not a promise for your lot.

sections.heading: A Reported 7.0 GPM Is a Starting Point, Not a Guarantee
sections.html:
The 1,415 wells with reported pump yields have a 7.0 gpm median, with the middle half at 4.0-10.0 gpm. Those rates can support household planning, but a reported drilling-time yield is not the same as a current sustained pumping test.

Reported yields fall under 1 gpm for 2% of wells, while 27% fall in the 1-5 gpm band. For a buyer, the lower-yield records are a reason to investigate recovery and storage needs before closing. A pressure tank alone does not solve inadequate well production. Ask for a test that documents pumping rate, drawdown and recovery, then have the pump and storage system matched to the results.

sections.heading: Water at 50 Feet Does Not Mean a 50-Foot Well
sections.html:
Only 307 records report a static water level. Their median is 50 feet below ground, with the middle half at 30-82 feet. Static level is where water rests in the well when it is not being pumped. It is not the total drilling depth or proof of how much water the well can deliver.

Decade medians were 35 feet in the 1960s and 1970s, 32 feet in the 1990s, 70 feet in the 2010s and 50 feet in the 2020s. That is not a steady decline. These grouped records do not establish a countywide water-table trend because they are not repeated measurements of the same wells under comparable conditions.

sections.heading: Gilpin's Permit Record Reflects Long-Established Well Use
sections.html:
Permit issuance was especially active in the 1970s, with 979 permits, and the 1990s, with 957. The records extend through 2025. Domestic and household use accounts for 92%, consistent with wells serving mountain properties rather than broad irrigation development.

The most active driller entries are C. R. Smith Drilling (Smith, Calvin R.), with 885 records; C R Smith Drilling Inc (Smith, Frank), with 645; and Ground Water Systems Inc (Wilson, Richard R.), with 415. These are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability.

Of 4,554 permitted wells, 3,267 are recorded as constructed. That difference should not be treated as a dry-hole count; a permit record alone does not establish construction or performance.

sections.heading: Budgeting the Hole and the Finished Gilpin County System
sections.html:
The local cost model uses $65-$100 per foot for drilling fractured granite and gneiss. At the 250-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $16,200-$25,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $22,200-$37,000.

Treat those figures as planning ranges, not a parcel-specific quote. Mountain access, required casing and grout, pump selection, and the route from the well to the house all affect the scope. Ask the driller to separate footage charges from completion equipment and explain what happens if the hole must go deeper. Coordinate driveway access and utility trenching before pricing the work, rather than assuming those items are straightforward.

sections.heading: Mining History and Low-Yield Risk Deserve Separate Checks
sections.html:
The supplied environmental mapping identifies 4,519 historic mine features, 42 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 30 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those are screening flags, not evidence that a particular Gilpin County well is contaminated. A PFAS sampling location also does not necessarily indicate a detection.

Review nearby site records and obtain current laboratory testing, including routine drinking-water tests and additional analytes guided by mining history or identified contamination. Inspect the wellhead, casing and surface drainage. Separately, assess production: fractured bedrock can produce a weak well or an unsuccessful hole. Before committing to a building layout, verify that the well, septic system and construction access can meet applicable siting requirements.

sections.heading: Before Buying a Lot Near Rollinsville or Black Hawk
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's DWR permit, completion report and pump records. Confirm the authorized uses rather than assuming a household well allows outdoor watering, livestock or additional dwellings. New permits depend on the parcel and applicable water rules; augmentation may be necessary where the proposed use requires it in an over-appropriated basin.

Compare neighboring wells around Rollinsville or Black Hawk before relying on broader figures from Clear Creek County or Boulder County. Favor nearby records with similar terrain and bedrock conditions. For an existing home, obtain a current yield test and water-quality results. For vacant land, have the proposed well location, septic area, driveway and house site reviewed together before finalizing the purchase.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Gilpin County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth in Gilpin County is 250 feet, and the middle half is 150-380 feet. Those figures come from 3,309 depth records. Fractured bedrock makes individual results variable, so use nearby completion reports to refine a bid and ask how additional footage will be priced.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Gilpin County?
faq.a: The drilling model is $65-$100 per foot in Gilpin County's fractured mountain bedrock. At the 250-foot median depth, the hole is about $16,200-$25,000; a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $22,200-$37,000. Get a site-specific quote that addresses access, casing and the utility route.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Gilpin County?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 7.0 gpm, with the middle half at 4.0-10.0 gpm. Among wells reporting yield, 2% are under 1 gpm. These records help screen a property, but a current pumping and recovery test is needed to assess household supply and any storage requirements.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Gilpin County?
faq.a: Safety has to be established for the individual well through laboratory testing. Mapping within about 10 miles includes 4,519 historic mine features and 42 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, but proximity does not prove contamination. Review nearby environmental records, inspect the well's condition and select tests appropriate to the property's potential exposures.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Gilpin County?
faq.a: The available records do not establish a steady countywide decline. Median static levels were 35 feet below ground in the 1960s, 70 feet in the 2010s and 50 feet in the 2020s. Only 307 wells report static levels, and the decade groups are not repeated measurements of the same wells.
